title: He missed the rest
hook: if told someone speaks ill of you, say: he didn't know my other faults (Enchiridion 33)

segments.voice: Yesterday: your own deeds and dangers, which please you more than your listeners. Your line was ask, don't tell. What question did you ask, and what did you hear? Day three hundred sixty-eight.

Your phone buzzes. A friend has sent a screenshot with three words above it: thought you should know. Someone has been saying things about you. Your face goes hot. Already you're drafting the reply in your head, point by point, with receipts. Epictetus knew this moment nearly two thousand years before screenshots, and in section thirty-three he hands his students a one-line answer for it. It's short, it's a little ridiculous, and it may be the best comeback in ancient philosophy. Today: he missed the rest.
screen: `THOUGHT YOU SHOULD KNOW.` → `ALREADY DRAFTING THE REPLY.` → `HE MISSED THE REST.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. If someone tells you that a certain person is speaking badly of you, Epictetus says, don't defend yourself against what was said. Instead, answer: he obviously didn't know my other faults, or he wouldn't have mentioned only these. Second, why it works. A defense keeps the argument alive. You go point by point, they answer, the circle grows. Epictetus' reply steps out of the contest entirely. It agrees, cheerfully, that you have faults, more than the critic knows, and so there's nothing left to fight about. The joke is on yourself, which is the one target that can't be hurt by it. Third, the Greek. The word he uses for defend yourself is the verb behind apologia, a speech of defense. It's the word in the title of Plato's Apology, where Socrates defends himself at his trial. Our English word apology grew from it, though it has drifted to mean saying sorry. Epictetus' advice, roughly: skip the apologia. Fourth, what it isn't. It isn't self-hatred, and it isn't ignoring a fair point. If the critic is right about something, you've learned something. If they're wrong, nothing that belongs to you has been touched. We met that idea a few weeks ago, with the insult: it's not the words that harm you, but your judgment that you've been harmed. Today's line is that idea with a grin on its face. It costs nothing. And it ends the conversation better than any receipt.
screen: `DON'T DEFEND YOURSELF.` · `HE DIDN'T KNOW MY OTHER FAULTS.` · `SKIP THE APOLOGIA.` · `A FAIR POINT TEACHES; A WRONG ONE CAN'T HARM.` · then, large: `HE MISSED THE REST.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and breathe. Bring to mind one criticism that still stings, something said about you or to you, recently or long ago. Notice where it lands in your body. Notice the urge to argue with it. Now try Epictetus' answer, quietly, inside: he missed the rest. You might even smile. See if the sting changes. If part of the criticism was fair, let that part stay, and let the rest go. The bell holds the time.
He missed the rest. Epictetus' answer to someone speaking ill of you: they didn't know my other faults, or they'd have mentioned those too. Today's word.
Your line: he missed the rest. If a criticism reaches you today, answer it with humor instead of a defense, out loud or just inside. Day three hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes answer reported criticism with self-deprecating humor, as Epictetus suggests, rather than defending themselves point by point.

original.note: Greek: a speech of defense. Epictetus uses the related verb: don't defend yourself.

trapdoor: what you thought: ignore your critics.
what it means: don't defend; agree, with a smile, that you have even more faults than they named.
what a scholar hears: the verb is the one behind apologia, the defense speech of Plato's Apology, here set aside for a joke.

notes: Enchiridion 33.9 paraphrased: if told someone speaks ill of you, do not defend yourself against what was said, but reply that he did not know your other faults, else he would not have mentioned these only. Confirm sub-section number.
Greek: the verb is ἀπολογέομαι ('do not defend yourself', μὴ ἀπολογοῦ). Confirm reading and that ἀπολογία is fair as the 'original' word.
